readiness-low.label: Foundation Builder
readiness-low.summary: Your current rhythm has a few useful signals, but the basics need more consistency before deeper tracking will feel helpful. Start with one simple meal rhythm and build from there.
keyPatterns: Meal timing is still inconsistent day to day
Protein anchors are easy to miss or skip
Observation habits are occasional rather than repeatable
firstFocusAreas: Notice the easiest time of day to improve
readiness-low.methodPositioning: Use the Method as a simple foundation-building path, not a strict overhaul.

page1.headline: You are building the foundation — and that is the right place to start.
body: Your answers suggest your eating rhythm is still taking shape. That is not a failure — it means the next step should be smaller and steadier, not a full tracking push.
Before deeper observation or logging feels useful, most people need one repeatable anchor: a first meal you can protect, a simple protein cue, and brief check-ins at an easy time of day.
This result is a readiness snapshot, not a verdict. Low readiness means we start smaller — not that you are behind.
snapshotBullets: Meal timing varies day to day
page1.meaningBody: You likely need more basic structure before guided tracking. That is a normal starting point — not a reason to skip ahead or overhaul everything at once.

page2.headline: Start with one rhythm, not a full reset.
body: When baseline habits are still forming, repetition beats intensity.
Pick one first meal you can repeat at a similar time most days. Add one reliable protein anchor there. Notice what feels easiest to improve first — that is your starting edge.
Keep other changes minimal until that rhythm feels familiar.
stepBullets: Notice the easiest time of day to improve

page3.problemHeadline: Most plans skip the baseline step.
problemBody: Generic nutrition advice often assumes you already have meal rhythm, planning habits, and observation skills in place.
When those foundations are still forming, jumping straight into tracking can feel overwhelming — and the data is harder to interpret.
Fine Diet starts differently: structure first, observation second, guided tracking when you are ready.
tryBullets: Protect one first meal at a similar time most days
Add one protein anchor you can repeat without stress
Resist changing multiple variables at once
page3.tryCloser: Small, repeatable steps build the baseline that makes tracking useful later.
page3.mechanismBodyTop: Rhythm reduces decision fatigue. Simple anchors build confidence without pressure.
page3.mechanismBodyBottom: When these habits feel familiar, tracking becomes a tool — not a burden.
methodBody: Fine Diet is built around observation and pattern recognition — not quick fixes or rigid rules.
Your readiness result helps us meet you where you are and sequence support appropriately.
methodLearnBullets: How to build meal rhythm without overhauling your life

readiness-building.label: Rhythm Builder
readiness-building.summary: You have a workable base. The next move is turning scattered healthy choices into a rhythm you can repeat on normal days, not just ideal ones.
keyPatterns: Some meal rhythm exists but is not yet steady
Protein and fiber show up sometimes, not reliably
Energy and appetite patterns are noticeable but not yet tracked
firstFocusAreas: Make protein and fiber easier to repeat
Track the patterns that change your energy and appetite
readiness-building.methodPositioning: Use the Method to turn good instincts into a repeatable eating rhythm.

page1.headline: You have a workable base — now build rhythm.
body: Your answers show partial habits: some meal timing, some planning, some observation. That is real progress.
The opportunity now is consistency — turning scattered healthy choices into a rhythm you can repeat on normal days, not just ideal ones.
You do not need perfection. You need a pattern you can return to when life gets busy.
This result reflects readiness to ramp up observation — not readiness to skip the basics.
snapshotBullets: Protein and fiber are sometimes present
Patterns are emerging but not yet tracked
page1.meaningBody: You are close and capable. The next step is structured observation — turning good instincts into a repeatable rhythm before full guided tracking.

page2.headline: Turn occasional habits into daily rhythm.
body: Pick the habit that is closest to automatic and make it non-negotiable for two weeks.
Stabilize meal timing where you can. Make protein and fiber easier to repeat. Start noticing which patterns shift your energy and appetite.
When rhythm feels familiar, light observation becomes much more useful.
stepBullets: Make protein and fiber easier to repeat
Track the patterns that change your energy and appetite

problemBody: Many people stall because they try to perfect every meal instead of repeating a few good patterns.
When habits are forming, the win is showing up — not optimizing every detail.
Fine Diet helps you build rhythm first, then layer in guided observation and tracking when the foundation holds.
tryBullets: Make your strongest existing meal-time habit non-negotiable for two weeks
Add one protein or fiber anchor you can repeat on normal days
Start a simple observation log for energy and appetite
page3.tryCloser: Steady repetition is what turns partial habits into baseline readiness.
page3.mechanismBodyTop: When meals follow a pattern, observation data becomes meaningful instead of noisy.
page3.mechanismBodyBottom: You are close — consistency is the bridge to guided tracking.
methodBody: Fine Diet sequences support to match your readiness. You are in the building phase — structure and observation come before full tracking.
Your result helps us recommend the right pace for your next step.

readiness-ready.label: Ready for Guided Observation
readiness-ready.summary: You are in a good position to use structured tracking and reflection. The next step is observing your patterns closely enough to make confident adjustments.
keyPatterns: Protein, fiber, and planning show up on most days
You notice how meals affect energy, hunger, and follow-through
firstFocusAreas: Track what you eat with context
Connect meals to energy, hunger, and consistency
Use weekly reflection to choose the next adjustment
readiness-ready.methodPositioning: Use the Method as a guided observation layer for users ready to learn from their own patterns.

page1.headline: You are ready for guided observation — not perfection.
body: Your answers show consistent meal rhythm, regular planning, and established observation habits.
That is the foundation Fine Diet is built on. You do not need to overhaul your routine before starting.
Your next step is structured tracking and reflection — observing your patterns closely enough to make confident adjustments.
This result confirms readiness for guided practice, not that every habit is locked in forever.
page1.meaningBody: You have enough baseline structure to start guided observation. Tracking can build on what you already do — practical and test-oriented, not a full reset.

page2.headline: Start guided observation from where you are.
body: Your existing rhythm is an asset — use it as the foundation for tracking.
Log meals with context for one week. Connect what you eat to energy, hunger, and consistency. Use weekly reflection to choose the next small adjustment.
Fine Diet Method sequencing will help you interpret what you observe and decide what to change.
stepBullets: Track what you eat with context
Connect meals to energy, hunger, and consistency
Use weekly reflection to choose the next adjustment

page3.problemHeadline: You do not need to start over.
problemBody: Many programs assume you need a reset before you can make progress. Your readiness result says otherwise.
You already have structure. The Fine Diet Method helps you use observation and pattern recognition to decide what to adjust — not to start from zero.
Guided tracking builds on your baseline, it does not replace it.
tryBullets: Begin a one-week observation log using your current rhythm
Note energy, hunger, and consistency without changing meals yet
Review your log before deciding on any adjustments
page3.tryCloser: Your baseline is the starting line — not something to fix first.
page3.mechanismBodyTop: Consistent rhythm makes tracking data meaningful. Observation turns data into insight.
page3.mechanismBodyBottom: Fine Diet helps you interpret patterns and sequence changes — not impose a one-size-fits-all plan.
methodBody: Fine Diet is observation-first nutrition guidance. You are ready to begin the guided pathway built on the structure you already have.
Your readiness result confirms you can start without a full reset.
